traits: Blades fold or roll lengthwise and turn a dull blue-gray-green before browning
Footprints or mower tracks stay visible in the turf longer than usual
Damage often starts on high spots, slopes or near sidewalks and driveways

copy.what_it_means: Folded, blue-gray blades and lingering footprints suggest wilt in this spot, most often from too little water, but a photo cannot tell drought apart from other causes of wilt. Watering the spot for a few days and watching for green-up, or a technician checking the irrigation coverage, confirms it.
copy.fact: Turf under drought stress conserves water by rolling its blades inward, which changes how light reflects off the leaf.

tech_notes: Check irrigation zone coverage and run time before assuming a disease; footprint test helps separate this from disease-related thinning.

symptoms: Blades fold or roll lengthwise and turn a dull blue-gray-green before browning
Footprints or mower tracks stay visible in the turf longer than usual

required_signature.text: A water response check settles this: water the spot for two to three days and watch for green-up. Lingering footprints point to wilt of any cause, not drought specifically.
elements: Blades fold or roll lengthwise and turn a dull blue-gray-green before browning
Footprints or mower tracks stay visible in the turf longer than usual

field_tests.name: Water response check
field_tests.how: Water the affected spot well for two to three days and watch for green-up.
field_tests.reads_as: Green-up within a few days points to drought stress; no response points elsewhere.

field_tests.name: Footprint test
field_tests.how: Walk across the lawn and look back after a few minutes.
field_tests.reads_as: Lingering footprints point to wilt, usually from water; a green-up after watering settles it. Grass that springs back quickly points elsewhere.

differentials.difference: Drought stress is uniform and blue-gray, greening up within days of water; large patch keeps a rotted ring at the base even after watering.
differentials.next_observation: Water the dry-looking edge for a few days and recheck, or a technician checks the leaf bases.

differentials.difference: Drought stress greens up within days of watering; take-all root rot roots stay short, black and rotted regardless of water.
differentials.next_observation: Water the area for a few days and recheck, or pull a plug to check the roots.

differentials.difference: Drought stress shows blue-gray, folded blades across dry zones; mower scalping is a uniform tan, stubbly cut appearing right after a mow.
differentials.next_observation: Check whether the discoloration followed a recent mow or a dry, sunny spell.

differentials.difference: Chinch bug damage is confined to hot, sunny areas near pavement with insects present; drought stress responds to watering within days.
differentials.next_observation: Pour soapy water on the edge of the patch and watch for small black-and-white bugs climbing up in a few minutes, or a technician checks.

condition.recovery_note: Color and green-up often follow within 2-3 weeks once watering is corrected.

traits: Turf stays a dull, light green, thin and shallow-rooted despite frequent watering
Soil feels spongy and wet, sometimes with algae or moss on the surface
Turf is more prone to disease and weeds that favor wet soil

copy.what_it_means: Dull, thin, shallow-rooted turf with spongy, wet soil suggests overwatering. It does not rule out a drainage problem; an irrigation can test measures how much water the zone is actually getting.
copy.fact: Grass roots need oxygen in the soil just as much as water, so soil that stays saturated can actually starve the roots even though the plant looks well watered.

tech_notes: Check run times and frequency against the season; reduce frequency and water deeper, less often to encourage deeper roots.

symptoms: Turf stays a dull, light green, thin and shallow-rooted despite frequent watering
Soil feels spongy and wet, sometimes with algae or moss on the surface

required_signature.text: An irrigation can test settles this: water measuring more than about half to three-quarters of an inch per run, or standing afterwards, confirms overwatering.
elements: Turf stays a dull, light green, thin and shallow-rooted despite frequent watering

field_tests.name: Irrigation can test
field_tests.how: Place a few shallow cans across the zone while it runs, then measure the water depth in each.
field_tests.reads_as: Water measuring more than about half to three-quarters of an inch per run, or standing afterwards, points to overwatering.

differentials.difference: Overwatering causes a dull, thin, waterlogged lawn overall without mushrooms in a ring; fairy ring shows mushrooms or a dark green band in a circle or arc.
differentials.next_observation: A photo of the ring pattern, or an irrigation can test checking how much water the zone gets.

differentials.difference: Overwatering alone recovers once watering is corrected; pythium root rot needs a technician to check the roots even after watering is fixed.
differentials.next_observation: An irrigation can test to check watering, alongside a root check by a technician.

differentials.difference: Overwatering causes general thin, waterlogged turf without distinct spots; dog urine spots are small, sharply defined dead circles with a dark green rim.
differentials.next_observation: A wider photo checking whether the damage is general or in small, distinct spots.

condition.recovery_note: Density and root depth often improve over 60-90 days once watering frequency is reduced.

traits: Blades grow longer and thinner reaching for light, weakening the turf over time
Bare or thin spots develop under tree canopy or building shadow, inviting weeds
Turf in the same spot is more easily hurt by foot traffic and slow to recover

copy.what_it_means: Stretched, thin blades and bare spots lining up with tree canopy or building shade suggest shade thinning. Turfgrass generally needs more sun than a heavily shaded spot provides; a ground cover or mulch bed is often a better long-term fit than more lawn care.
copy.fact: Grass grown in shade stretches its blades longer trying to catch more light, which actually drains the plant's energy reserves faster than staying short.

tech_notes: In heavily shaded areas, growing turfgrass is often not realistic long-term regardless of species or care. Blades also grow longer and thinner reaching for light, which weakens the turf over time.

symptoms: Blades grow longer and thinner reaching for light
Bare or thin spots develop under tree canopy or building shadow, inviting weeds

required_signature.text: A wide photo of the thin or bare area showing it lines up with tree canopy or building shade.
elements: Bare or thin spots develop under tree canopy or building shadow, inviting weeds

differentials.difference: Shade thinning follows the shadow of a tree or structure with stretched, thin blades; compaction wear follows a foot-traffic path or gate regardless of light.
differentials.next_observation: A wider photo checking whether the thin area matches a shade pattern or a traffic path.

differentials.difference: Shade thinning shows stretched, thin blades and bare spots under canopy with no pustules; rust shows orange, powdery pustules on the blade.
differentials.next_observation: A close-up of the blade surface checking for pustules.

condition.recovery_note: Density rarely improves without more light; fill-in elsewhere can take 60-90 days once shade is reduced.

traits: Thin, worn or bare turf along a consistent foot path, gate or parking pattern
Water tends to pool or run off rather than soak in on the worn area
Soil here is noticeably harder to probe than the surrounding lawn

copy.what_it_means: A worn strip of thin turf that follows a foot path, gate or parking pattern suggests compaction from repeated traffic. Aeration and rerouting traffic where possible are the realistic fixes; a technician can advise if the worn area keeps expanding.
copy.fact: Compacted soil holds less oxygen for roots, which is why worn paths often stay thin even after traffic stops for a while.

tech_notes: A soil probe or shovel test (hard to push in past a few inches) confirms compaction; plug aeration is the usual remedy in an existing lawn. Water also tends to pool or run off rather than soak in on the worn area, another clue.

symptoms: Thin, worn or bare turf along a consistent foot path, gate or parking pattern

required_signature.text: A wide photo of the worn strip showing it follows a foot path, gate or parking pattern.
elements: Thin, worn or bare turf along a consistent foot path, gate or parking pattern

differentials.difference: Compaction wear follows a repeated traffic path regardless of light; shade thinning follows the shadow of a tree or structure with stretched, thin blades.
differentials.next_observation: A wider photo checking whether the thin area matches a traffic path or a shade pattern.

differentials.difference: Compaction wear follows a repeated traffic path regardless of mowing; mower scalping is a uniform tan cut appearing right after a single low mow.
differentials.next_observation: Check whether the thin area is a walking path or matches a recent mow.

condition.recovery_note: Density can improve over 60-90 days once aeration and traffic patterns are addressed.

traits: Leaf tips and margins burn brown or tan, often worse on the side facing onshore wind or salt spray
Leaves may look scorched, dry and unusually brittle for the season
Damage is often one-sided, matching the direction the salt exposure comes from

copy.what_it_means: Brown, scorched tips and margins worse on one side can suggest salt injury, often onshore wind, brackish irrigation, storm surge or heavy fertilizer, but a photo cannot rule out other causes. A technician checks the likely source; rinsing foliage and choosing salt-tolerant plants are the realistic fixes.
copy.fact: Salt injury often shows up worse on the side of a plant facing the wind or the water, since that side takes the brunt of the wind-blown salt spray.

tech_notes: Consider the irrigation water source (well or reclaimed water salinity) and onshore wind carrying Gulf spray, as well as storm surge or a recent heavy fertilizer application; road de-icing salt is not a factor in Southwest Florida.

symptoms: Leaf tips and margins burn brown or tan, often worse on the side facing onshore wind or salt spray
Leaves may look scorched, dry and unusually brittle for the season

required_signature.text: A photo cannot rule out other causes on its own; a technician checks the one-sided pattern against the likely salt source.
elements: Leaf tips and margins burn brown or tan, often worse on the side facing onshore wind or salt spray
Leaves may look scorched, dry and unusually brittle for the season

differentials.difference: Salt injury browns tips and margins, worse facing onshore wind or spray; anthracnose causes scattered lesions with a yellow halo and can cause dieback.
differentials.next_observation: A wider photo of the whole plant checking whether the burn follows the side facing onshore wind or salt spray.

differentials.difference: Salt injury browns tips and margins, worse facing onshore wind or spray; leaf spot fungi cause scattered round spots across the leaf, not just the margin.
differentials.next_observation: A wider photo of the whole plant checking whether the burn follows the side facing onshore wind or salt spray.

differentials.difference: Both can look one-sided in a photo; leaf scorch spreads from one branch over months to years, while salt injury tracks wind or spray exposure.
differentials.next_observation: A technician tracks whether the browning spreads from one branch over time, or tests for the bacterium.

condition.recovery_note: New growth is often unaffected; existing scorched leaves do not recover but usually shed over a few weeks.

traits: Leaflets or leaves browned or blackened, worst on the most exposed growth
Some leaves look water-soaked and others brown or black on the exposed parts of the plant
Damage is worse on plants in open, unprotected spots than those under canopy or near a building

copy.what_it_means: Leaves that look water-soaked, then brown or black, within days of a cold snap suggest cold damage, worse on exposed growth. On a palm, a spear leaf that pulls free after a freeze needs a technician right away. Leave damaged leaves in place until the cold season passes; removing them too soon can do more harm.
copy.fact: Even fully dead, brown palm fronds still insulate the bud from further cold, which is one reason it pays to wait before cutting them off.

tech_notes: Do not remove damaged palm fronds until the danger of further cold has passed and 2-3 new leaves have emerged; check water needs after a freeze since roots may be too cold to function normally. On a palm, cold can also kill the spear leaf itself, not just the older fronds.

symptoms: Leaflets or leaves browned or blackened, worst on the most exposed growth
Some leaves look water-soaked and others brown or black on the exposed parts of the plant

required_signature.text: A wide photo showing water-soaked and browned or blackened leaves, worst on the most exposed growth.
elements: Leaflets or leaves browned or blackened, worst on the most exposed growth
Some leaves look water-soaked and others brown or black on the exposed parts of the plant

differentials.difference: Cold damage can also kill the spear leaf after a hard freeze, so a pulled-free spear does not by itself separate it from bud rot; both need a technician.
differentials.next_observation: A technician checks the bud and whether other fronds also show cold injury, since a pulled-free spear can mean either.

differentials.difference: Cold damage appears within days of a cold snap and can affect many fronds at once; potassium deficiency develops gradually and stays on the oldest fronds only.
differentials.next_observation: A technician checks how many fronds are affected and whether the damage lines up with a recent cold snap.

condition.recovery_note: New growth over the following months shows whether the plant has recovered; damaged leaves do not green back up.

traits: Leaf scorch, wilting or undersized new leaves on a fresh planting (stakes, new mulch ring or exposed root ball)
Premature fall color or early leaf drop out of season on a new planting
Growth stalls or slows noticeably compared to before the plant was moved

copy.what_it_means: Scorch, wilting or stalled growth on a recently planted tree or shrub suggests transplant shock while the root system reestablishes. Light, frequent watering is often the fix, but if the soil is already wet a technician checks drainage and planting depth first; symptoms usually ease as the plant settles in.
copy.fact: A transplanted tree or shrub loses much of its fine root system in the move, which is why light, frequent watering matters more in the first few months than afterward.

tech_notes: Roughly 2-3 irrigations per week for the first few months after planting is typical guidance if the soil is not already wet; confirm the plant is not also deep-planted, root-bound or sitting in poor drainage. Premature fall color or early leaf drop out of season can be another clue.

symptoms: Leaf scorch, wilting or undersized new leaves on a fresh planting (stakes, new mulch ring or exposed root ball)

required_signature.text: A wide photo of the struggling plant showing signs of a new installation (stakes, a fresh mulch ring or the root ball edge) and whether the soil looks wet or dry.
elements: Leaf scorch, wilting or undersized new leaves on a fresh planting (stakes, new mulch ring or exposed root ball)

differentials.difference: Transplant shock affects a recently moved plant and often improves within months; root rot can affect an established plant and worsens with wet soil.
differentials.next_observation: A technician checks the roots and confirms how recently the plant was planted.

differentials.difference: Transplant shock eases within months on its own; a mulch volcano keeps stressing the plant until the excess mulch or soil is pulled back.
differentials.next_observation: A photo of the trunk base checking whether the root flare is visible or buried.

condition.recovery_note: Most new plantings recover over a few months as roots reestablish, once watering is consistent.

traits: Mulch or soil piled against the trunk, burying the root flare where the trunk widens at the base
Slow, stunted growth with the tree or shrub failing to establish for no obvious reason
Bark at the buried trunk base may stay damp, soft or discolored

copy.what_it_means: Mulch or soil piled against the trunk, burying the root flare, suggests a mulch volcano or a plant set too deep at installation. Pulling mulch and excess soil back from the trunk so the root flare shows is the realistic fix.
copy.fact: A buried trunk stays damp and low on oxygen, conditions that favor rot and can also invite insects that would not otherwise reach the trunk.

tech_notes: Keep mulch 2-3 inches deep with a gap of roughly a foot around the trunk of an established tree; check for the root flare when in doubt. Slow, stunted growth with the plant failing to establish for no obvious reason is another clue.

signs: Mulch or soil piled against the trunk, burying the root flare where the trunk widens at the base

required_signature.text: A photo of the trunk base showing mulch or soil piled against the trunk with the root flare buried.
elements: Mulch or soil piled against the trunk, burying the root flare where the trunk widens at the base

differentials.difference: A buried root flare confirms deep planting, but does not rule out root rot at the same time; a technician checks the roots regardless.
differentials.next_observation: A technician digs at the roots to check for rot even when the flare is visibly buried.

differentials.difference: A mulch volcano keeps stressing a plant of any age until corrected; transplant shock affects a newly moved plant and eases within months on its own.
differentials.next_observation: A photo of the trunk base checking whether the root flare is visible or buried.

differentials.difference: A mulch volcano buries the trunk base under soil or mulch with no visible wound; trimmer bark damage shows a scraped or gouged wound with bark missing.
differentials.next_observation: A close-up of the trunk base checking for a bare wound versus buried mulch.

condition.recovery_note: Growth often improves within a few months once the root flare is uncovered and mulch depth is corrected.
